2022-50051.text:
## How they got there
Real Madrid won the 2021-22 Champions League, beating Liverpool 1-0 in the final after navigating the group stage. Their profile was defined by exceptional ball retention and discipline, recording 670 passes per game, which was better than 100% of that season's teams. They also committed just 7.8 fouls per game, a figure that was better than 97% of their peers, while holding a pre-season UEFA club coefficient of 127.0 points, better than 97% of teams.

## Would the model have picked them?
The model would not have picked them, as it ranked them 5th, outside its top two. Its probability of reaching the final was 19.0%, compared to the 12.5% base rate for a random knockout team. The stage nearest to the model's expectation of 2.04 was the semi-finals. The stat that pushed the prediction up most was attacks per game, with a SHAP contribution of 0.37, while the stat that pushed it down most was long passes (% of passes), with a contribution of -0.08.

## Weak spots
Their long passes (% of passes) stood at 8.8, a value that was better than 6% of that season's teams. The distance covered per game (km) was 110.3, which was better than 12% of that season's teams. Opponent shots per game (lower is better) was 9.0, a figure that was better than 44% of that season's teams.

synthesis.text:
## Why the best teams win

The model achieved a Brier score of 0.098 against a base-rate Brier score of 0.103. Its Brier skill was 0.05, with a 95% interval of [-0.04, 0.13]. Because this interval includes zero, the model's edge on that measure is inconclusive. It placed 46.7% of actual finalists in its top 4, compared to 23.9% for a random ranking. The 95% interval for this share is [30.0, 60.0], which lies entirely above the random share. The mean Spearman correlation was 0.45 [0.34, 0.54] and the AUC was 0.73 [0.61, 0.83]. The model learns from 256 knockout team-seasons, utilizing each team's group or league-phase statistics to predict their subsequent performance in the tournament.

Attacks per game (importance 0.229) and goal difference per game (0.198) are robust stats where higher values help. Long passes (0.135) is conditional, meaning its direction holds only with other stats fixed, as it points the other way on its own. Passes per game (0.119) is robust, while fouls committed (0.094) is model-dependent, making its direction unstable. Shot conversion (0.086) is also conditional. Feature-set comparisons show style (Spearman 0.39) outperforms results (0.30) and pedigree (0.27). However, their 95% intervals overlap, so differences between these groups are tentative. The full set (0.45) performs slightly better than style alone, but the overlapping confidence ranges prevent definitive claims about which group matters most for deep runs.

## Winners vs runners-up

Comparing group-phase stats, the first four stats by Holm-adjusted p-value show specific patterns. Pre-season UEFA club coefficient had a mean difference of 0.57 z-scores with a p-value of 0.111. Fouls committed per game showed a mean difference of -1.13 z-scores with a p-value of 0.181. Shots per game had a mean difference of 0.79 z-scores with a p-value of 0.292. Finally, pass accuracy had a mean difference of 0.76 z-scores with a p-value of 0.422. These values represent the average difference between the winner and runner-up, standardized by the distribution of all finalists in the dataset.

In the 15 finals, the winner was higher on pre-season UEFA club coefficient in 13 instances and lower in 2. For fouls committed, the winner was higher in 2 finals and lower in 12, with one tie. The winner recorded more shots per game in 11 finals and fewer in 2, with two ties. The winner had higher pass accuracy in 12 finals and lower in 3. None of these differences were significant, as all Holm-adjusted p-values exceeded the 0.05 threshold. The data indicates that while winners often had better pre-season coefficients and higher shot volumes, these advantages were not statistically distinct from runners-up in the group phase.
